newsitem.title: USA: U.S., France report differences on new air accord.
newsitem.headline: U.S., France report differences on new air accord.

text.p: France and the United States ended three days of talks on a new air services agreement Thursday with substantial differences remaining on how liberal the agreement should be, U.S. and French officials said.
They also said there were differences on its timing.
But both sides said they would meet again soon, probably before summer, in Paris.

The U.S. officials said the United States proposed a traditional free market "open skies" agreement to be phased in over three years, but France countered with something short of an free market accord to be phased in over nine years.

Free market accords the United States already has with countries that include Canada and Germany end all restrictions on routes and their frequencies and allow carriers to fly to the other country and "beyond."

But the French officials rejected the "beyond" rights, saying the benefits of those rights for U.S. carriers flying to France were far more valuable than similar rights for a French carrier to fly to the United States and beyond.
The United States said in a statement "there were substantial differences of positions" between the two sides, although further talks would be held.
Michel Guyard, director of air transport in the French directorate general of civil aviation, said the nine years was for France to become more competitive in trans-Atlantic air services.
He said Air France was rebuilding, and since 1992 had increased its share of the U.S.-French market to 40 percent from 30 percent.

Guyard said the coming rounds of talks with the United States would clarify the outstanding issues, including routes to be flown between the two countries, their frequencies and "code-sharing" marketing agreements.

There is now no bilateral air services agreement between the United States and France. France ended the accord in 1993 on grounds the United States wanted too many new routes for its many major carriers serving France.
They said this would create an imbalance of aviation services, with financially struggling Air France the only major French carrier serving the United States.
In the absence of a bilateral agreement, the United States and France have been negotiating routes and frequencies on a seasonal basis.
